..
Tuesday evening through Wednesday: A broad upper-level trough 
remains over the eastern Pacific, directing shortwaves into 
British Columbia and the Inland Northwest. These shortwaves will
bring passing high clouds at times through Wednesday, but are 
not expected to produce any precipitation. Afternoon highs will 
cool by 3-8 degrees from Tuesday to Wednesday, bringing 
afternoon highs into the low to mid 70s for most locations. 
Another round of breezy winds is expected Wednesday afternoon 
and evening across much of the region. Winds will be out of the 
southwest with sustained speeds of 10-15 mph and gusts up to 25 
mph.

Thursday through Saturday: A shortwave dropping down from the 
Gulf of Alaska into the offshore trough on Thursday will dig 
into the base of the trough, stretching it meridionally and 
temporarily bringing higher heights back over the eastern third 
of WA and the ID panhandle. These higher heights will briefly 
warm temperatures by 5-10 degrees in the aforementioned areas on
Thursday before the cooling trend resumes Friday and Saturday. 
Further west over Central WA, temperatures will remain largely 
unchanged from Wednesday into Thursday.

The offshore trough tracks inland Thursday night into Friday, 
sending a more robust cold front through the Inland Northwest 
Friday morning into Friday afternoon. With the cold front 
passage will come gusty winds, noticeably cooler temperatures, 
rain, scattered thunderstorms, and potential for high mountain 
snow. Models have come into better agreement on when the front 
will arrive and how quickly it will traverse the region,
depicting a swift frontal passage during peak heating hours on 
Friday. This has a couple of implications regarding the impacts
we'll see with the front. A frontal passage during peak heating
hours will mean steeper lapse rates will be in place, resulting
in a more unstable atmosphere. This is favorable for 
thunderstorm development AND for higher winds aloft to mix down 
to the surface.

Thus, chances for wind gusts of at least 20 mph, 30 mph, and 40
mph have continued to trend up regionwide with each consecutive
model run. The latest probabilities from the NBM show a 90-100%
chance for wind gusts of at least 20 mph, a 40-90% chance for 
30 mph, and a 20-40% chance for 40 mph. In general, the highest 
chances fall over the Columbia Basin, Waterville Plateau, and 
Lewiston-Clarkston Valley, while the lowest chances fall over 
the northern mountains and ID Panhandle. For the windiest 
locations including the lee of the Cascades, Waterville Plateau,
central Columbia Basin, and Lewiston- Clarkston Valley, there 
is a 15-30% chance of wind gusts hitting 50 mph. 

The end-of-week weather system will also deliver cooler 
temperatures with highs cooling from the 70s and low 80s 
Wednesday and Thursday into the upper 50s and 60s Friday through
the weekend. Overnight temperatures will decrease as well with 
widespread lows in the mid 30s to mid 40s starting Friday 
night. Some mountain valleys may be flirting with freezing 
overnight temperatures heading into the weekend. 

As for precipitation, ensembles are indicating an 80-100% 
chance for at least 0.10" along the Cascade Crest and mountains 
of NE WA and N ID by Saturday morning. The potential outcomes 
for these areas are as high as 0.75 inches or more. These
probabilities and amounts have trended up since yesterday. This
could equate to several inches of snow for some of the highest 
peaks. Latest guidance has continued to increase the chances 
for 0.10" of rain for lower elevations as well. Locations 
including Wenatchee, Ephrata, Spokane, Pullman, Lewiston, and 
Kellogg now have a 50-80% chance of receiving at least 0.10" of 
rain.

In addition to an upward trend in precipitation amounts, there
has also been an upward trend in chances for thunderstorms
Friday afternoon. There are now thunderstorm chances regionwide
ranging from 15-30%. The highest chances will be over north-
central WA.

Snow levels in the Cascades will drop near 6500 feet Friday and
will further decrease to around 5000 feet Friday night into 
Saturday morning. Those venturing into the high country should 
be prepared for cooler temperatures and wet conditions. At this 
time, snow accumulations look light, but a few of the highest 
peaks near the immediate Cascade crest could pick up several 
inches. 

Sunday onward: Confidence in the details of the forecast 
decreases Sunday into next week, but generally temperatures look
to stay in the 60s with periodic chances for mountain showers. 
/Fewkes
